passages.t: The song of Moses and of the Lamb
passages.happening:
John sees one more sign in heaven: “Then I saw another great and marvelous sign in heaven: seven angels with the seven final plagues, with which the wrath of God is completed” (verse 1).

Before the angels do anything, he sees a crowd. “And I saw something like a sea of glass mixed with fire, beside which stood those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name. They were holding harps from God” (verse 2).

He hears what they sing, “the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb” (verse 3): “Great and wonderful are Your works, O Lord God Almighty! Just and true are Your ways, O King of the nations! Who will not fear You, O Lord, and glorify Your name? For You alone are holy. All nations will come and worship before You, for Your righteous acts have been revealed” (verses 3-4).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 14 gave a glimpse of the end. Chapter 15 sets up the last series of seven, the bowls, which chapter 16 will pour out. It is the shortest chapter in Revelation, and most of it is worship. Every series of judgments in the book is framed by worship, and here the singing comes first.

The plagues are called ‘final’ because with them ‘the wrath of God is completed’. The Greek verb, teleō, means to finish or bring to its end. It is the verb John's Gospel uses as Jesus' work on the cross nears its end. The wrath of God in Scripture is not a fit of temper. It is his settled opposition to evil, and in these plagues it is brought to completion.

The sea of glass stood before the throne in chapter 4. Now it is mixed with fire, and the singers stand beside it. The picture is the Red Sea. After Israel crossed and saw Pharaoh's army drowned, Moses and the people sang on the shore. For Jews under Roman rule, the exodus was the great story of God's rescue from an empire, kept every year at Passover. For small churches in cities devoted to the emperor, this scene said that their rescue was as sure as Israel's.

The singers are ‘those who had conquered the beast’. In chapter 13 the beast was permitted to conquer the saints. Here the same people are called the conquerors. They won as the Lamb won, by staying faithful.

Their song is ‘the song of Moses and of the Lamb’. This is the only time Revelation names Moses. It joins Israel's rescue from Egypt and the rescue that came through Jesus into one story and one song. Paul calls Christ ‘our Passover lamb’ (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Notice what the song is about. It does not mention the singers, their suffering or their victory. It does not even name the Lamb. It praises God: his works, his ways, his holiness. And it looks outward with hope. ‘All nations will come and worship before You.’ On the edge of the last judgments, the song of the saved is still a song about the nations turning to God.
passages.ot:
The first song of Moses was sung on the shore: “Then Moses and the Israelites sang this song to the LORD: ‘I will sing to the LORD, for He is highly exalted. The horse and rider He has thrown into the sea’” (Exodus 15:1). It asked, “Who among the gods is like You, O LORD? Who is like You—majestic in holiness, revered with praises, performing wonders?” (Exodus 15:11).

The song in Revelation is woven from many Old Testament lines rather than quoting Exodus. “Great are the works of the LORD” (Psalm 111:2). Moses' second song says of God, “all His ways are just” (Deuteronomy 32:4). Jeremiah asks, “Who would not fear You, O King of nations?” (Jeremiah 10:7). And the psalm promises, “All the nations You have made will come and bow before You, O Lord, and they will glorify Your name” (Psalm 86:9).
passages.asks: Ask what it would mean to praise God before your own story is settled, as these singers do on the far shore before the last plagues fall. Ask whether your worship is mostly about what God has done for you, or about who he is. And ask whether you still hope, as this song does, that the nations will come to worship.

passages.t: The temple opened, and the seven bowls
passages.happening:
“After this I looked, and the temple—the tabernacle of the Testimony—was opened in heaven” (verse 5).

“And out of the temple came the seven angels with the seven plagues, dressed in clean and bright linen and girded with golden sashes around their chests” (verse 6).

“Then one of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God, who lives forever and ever” (verse 7).

“And the temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from His power; and no one could enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The temple in heaven is called ‘the tabernacle of the Testimony’. The tabernacle was the tent Israel carried through the wilderness. It was named for the Testimony, the tablets of God's covenant law kept inside the ark. By John's day no tabernacle had stood for centuries, and if the book was written after AD 70 the temple in Jerusalem was gone too. John sees the true sanctuary in heaven, which the letter to the Hebrews says the earthly one copied.

The judgments come out of that sanctuary. They come from the place of God's covenant law and God's presence, not from chance or from some power outside his rule.

The seven angels are dressed like priests, in clean bright linen with golden sashes. The risen Christ wore a golden sash in 1:13. The bowls are golden bowls, the shallow dishes used for offerings in temple worship. In 5:8 golden bowls held incense, which is the prayers of the saints. Now golden bowls hold God's wrath. Many readers see the link as deliberate. The last judgments are, in part, God's answer to his people's long prayers for justice, the prayer of the martyrs under the altar who asked, ‘How long?’ (6:10).

The bowls are handed over by one of the four living creatures, who stand around the throne and never stop calling God holy. And God is named again as the one ‘who lives forever and ever’. The empire that seemed to last for ever does not. God does.

Then the temple fills with smoke from God's glory and power, and no one can enter until the plagues are done. When the tabernacle was finished, and again when Solomon's temple was dedicated, the glory of the LORD filled it, and no one could go in. Isaiah saw the temple filled with smoke when he saw the LORD on his throne. The smoke speaks of God's holiness: his majesty is too great to approach. What is about to happen comes from that holiness, and it will be finished before the way is open again.
passages.ot:
The glory filled the tent in the wilderness: “Moses was unable to enter the Tent of Meeting because the cloud had settled on it, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (Exodus 40:35). It filled Solomon's temple, “so that the priests could not stand there to minister because of the cloud; for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD” (1 Kings 8:11). And in Isaiah's vision, “the temple was filled with smoke” (Isaiah 6:4).

The Testimony is the Law's name for the tablets of the covenant: “And place inside the ark the Testimony, which I will give you” (Exodus 25:16).
passages.hard:
The ‘final’ plagues: do the bowls come last in time, after the seals and trumpets, or do they tell the same story again?

Readers divide here, as they do over the seals and trumpets, and these notes do not choose. One view reads the three series in order: the seventh seal holds the seven trumpets, and the seventh trumpet holds the seven bowls, so the bowls are the last events before the end. Many futurists hold a form of this view. Another view, going back to Victorinus of Pettau, reads the three series as covering the same span, each told with greater force, and each ending at the final judgment. Those who hold it point out that the first four bowls strike the same places as the first four trumpets, earth, sea, rivers and sun, but now in full measure rather than in part. Some combine the two, and see both progress and overlap.

On either view, ‘final’ means that this series of judgments has a limit and an end, set by God. And the chapter that announces it is filled with a song about the nations coming to worship.
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that the bowls of wrath are golden bowls like the ones that held the saints' prayers. Ask how you hold together God's holiness, which no one can approach, and the Lamb, who opened the way to him. And ask what prayers for justice you have stopped praying because you thought God was not listening.
